title: Chapter 8 — The Quiet Hour
text:
Nobody talked on the way back.

Stash drove. Third gear the whole way through West Town, rain hammering the roof in a rhythm that almost sounded like pattern. Ledger held the cases on his lap. He didn't need to — the floor was fine, the locks were fine — but he did it anyway, and nobody said anything about it. The elevated passed overhead in sections. Sodium light dropped orange bars across the windshield, across Ledger's hands, across the shape in the back that none of them looked at.

The tremor was still in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s wrists. The blade had picked it up between <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s shoulder housings. He flexed his right hand once and let it go. It didn't go.

All he wanted now was to get home, lock the door, and make the shaking stop before morning. That was the whole of it. Get inside, get quiet, get the hand to hold still.

He made himself think about the job instead. Not the woman — the job. She'd pulled a file out of an operator's head and carried it behind her eyes onto the dock. That was the thing <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> had come to collect. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would never know what was in it. You didn't keep that part. The client paid for the extraction, the extraction got done, and everything after belonged to someone else. The folder was still classified, still in Ledger's lap, still full of things that couldn't be discussed in a vehicle with two other people in it.

But he kept seeing the way she'd moved out there. She'd read the geometry the same second he did and never once asked him to check her. There was a word for what she'd been. He didn't say it in the van.

The city moved past in grayscale. Somewhere above them, the float layer hummed with the weight of money and distance. At the third light, Ledger made a sound — not quite a word, not quite a sigh. The kind of noise someone makes when they're running a number in their head and don't like where it lands. He didn't elaborate. Stash kept their eyes on the road.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the rain.

The relay stayed quiet the whole drive home.

Two nights after the dock, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s light was on across the hall.

He knew the rhythm of it — two steps and back, two steps and back, the way she moved between her bench and her terminal when she was in the middle of something. He stood in his doorway a moment. He did not knock. He went to bed.

He woke at 04:00 and lay in the dark until the gray at the window was enough to call it morning. His right hand wouldn't uncurl. He worked it open, joint by joint, until the rail-edge bruise across the heel of his palm stopped complaining. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s dressing was clean. It would hold. Under the rain there was the city's hum, that 19 Hz that lived in everything now, so constant you stopped hearing it until you did.

He made coffee. He drank it standing. He did not look at the relay.

By 07:30 he looked at the relay. No new jobs. The last client had paid up front — clean rate, clean scope, full deposit before entry. That was closed. Done. He read the empty queue through twice anyway, the way you check a lock you already know is locked.

He had <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s number. He called it. It rang four times. He almost hung up — the woman was seventy-nine, and it was barely eight, and there was no reason she'd want to hear from him. On the fifth ring the line clicked open, but she said nothing. He could hear her breathing, waiting, the counter's morning behind her — the hiss of the first pot, someone's stool scraping the floor. The words he'd rehearsed came apart in his mouth. He started twice. The silence stretched. He was asking her to stand up in front of the whole block for a girl she'd known three months, and he had no right, and they both knew it.

"You're bringing something or you're taking something," she said, not a question, the way she priced everything before it was named.

"Taking something."

"Thursday," she said, before he finished. "Six o'clock. Tell whoever she kept." A pause, not hesitation, just her thinking. "You come to the counter. You sit. You eat. You don't talk until the counter's empty. You understand?"

"I understand."

"Then we're done." The line went quiet.

He did not ask how she knew. She had run that counter for sixty years.

Forty people <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did not know.

Mrs. Okafor had a clipboard. She moved through the front room the way a good coordinator moves through a site — not hurrying, not stopping, handing a plate here, steering foot traffic there. She caught <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s eye once across the room, checked the new arrival against her list, found what she needed, and moved on. The hand she kept at her side was not entirely still.

His neuretics caught the frequency before he finished reading the room.

The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> was in the corner, in the chair closest to the window, back to the wall. Jaw set. Both hands flat on their thighs. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="816dbd83-fa5a-4ccb-9b58-b353707146d3">The Read</entity> was running open — nineteen hertz, the kind you feel in your back teeth, a hum leaking past whatever the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> was using to hold it in. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it and moved on. He'd worked around Psyks before. You could tell them by the way their attention moved through a space, not aggressive, just aware — aware of things that weren't visible, reading a room the way other people read a menu.

<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> was the only name he'd ever had for her, and it hadn't occurred to him to wonder if there was more underneath it. It took <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s phone call and a face in a printed notice to tell him what she actually was: a Read, and had been the whole three years he'd known her — sitting across a counter from him with a skill that could have told her anything she wanted about anyone in the room, and choosing, every time, to sell him parts instead. She had built a whole career out of being the kind of face a room rounds down to nothing. He had bought parts off her twice a month for three years and apparently never once really looked.

On a corkboard near the far window there were photographs. Most were printed on the standard quick-format feed, slick-edged, from a public output terminal. One was different. Paper, not plastfilm, a little smaller than the rest, the corners soft from handling. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> at maybe nineteen, laughing at something outside the frame. <entity repo="character" guid="019ed3a6-ffc1-7ac2-825f-35df50b2e510">Head</entity> tilted back, eyes nearly closed, caught mid-motion like the laugh was still happening. She was wearing something with color in it, a rust-red shirt, warm. The background was green — trees, maybe, or water, somewhere that wasn't concrete and neon. She looked like someone who had slept well and woken up to something good. The laugh was real — full, unguarded, her whole body in it. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at it a while. He reached to take it off the board.

Mrs. Okafor's hand closed gently around his wrist from behind, barely a weight.

"That one stays," she said, not looking at it.

She let go and moved on. He let his hand come back. He did not know that laugh. He knew <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s tells, her range, the exact angle she tilted her head when she was reading someone and the moment her face went flat when she was done. He had known her for three years and he did not know this, which meant it came from somewhere he had never been — a life she'd had before the work turned her into the person he knew. The two things would not fit in the same space: the woman laughing in the photograph and the operator who'd read the geometry of a dock the same second he did. She had been both of them the whole time, and he'd never known the first one existed. He had never made room for that version of her. Now he never would.

Mrs. Okafor was back at his left shoulder. She handed him a plate without asking — jollof rice, two pieces of chicken, a fold of flatbread — and turned to the next thing before he could take it.

He took it with both hands. The plate was warm. He stood there holding it.

He did not eat.

They came in ones and twos through the rain. Not the kind of crowd that advertises.

Ledger came first, because Ledger was always early and never explained it. He took the far end stool, ordered once, and didn't speak for an hour, which for Ledger was grief. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had seen Ledger work a dozen times — efficient, precise, the kind of operator who prices a job and executes it clean. He'd never seen him look like this: like someone had removed something essential and left the shape standing.

Stash came next, walking careful, their load invisible tonight. They sat beside <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> without asking and ate in silence, with the same precision they brought to everything. A woman <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew as Casing arrived with someone he didn't know, introduced neither of them, and ate two bowls with the steady efficiency of a person taking care of what needed taking care of.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> came from across the hall. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did not ask how she'd known about <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>. The two of them had crossed paths on a job before, the Mirrorwell run. That was how <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had ended up with the analog barometer that still sat at the far end of her bench — hadn't moved since, probably never would. She'd never explained how she got it. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> had never mentioned giving it. Some things between women in the work ran on lines <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't on.

He had come here to do one thing and one thing only: sit through the whole of it without breaking, stay until the last bowl was empty and see every one of them out the door, the way <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> would have wanted it done. That was the job tonight. Nothing more.

She sat at his shoulder and said nothing for a long time. Then: "She was good."

"Yeah," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know three people who are that good. Now I know two."

He didn't answer. There wasn't an answer the right size.

The others came after — faces from jobs <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had worked next to, not with; people from <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s side of things, names he didn't have, which was correct, which was how it worked. They came alone or in pairs, never announcing themselves, ordered tea or broth or nothing, and found a place to stand or sit. Nobody was loud. Nobody was performing. The weight of all that restraint pressed down like a physical thing; <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it in his shoulders. Nobody checked their phone. The relay stayed dark.

Forty people in a noodle counter on Halsted, eating broth in honor of a woman most of them had known by exactly one name, and every one of them understanding exactly what that meant.

Four seconds.

The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> lost containment and the hum spiked — not louder, deeper, the nineteen hertz thickening into something that sat in the chest. Three people near the window flinched without knowing why. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics lit with it, a quick static bloom at the edge of his array. He met the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity>'s eyes across the room. The jaw was still set, the hands still flat, but the eyes had gone wide and unfocused — the way eyes go when something is moving through a person that won't quite hold. He wanted the count. If he could hold the look long enough to time the slip — how many seconds the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> stayed under before hauling it back — he'd know how close this room was to going the way the photograph had gone. So he watched, and he counted. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held the look. The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> pulled it back, hauling it in the way you haul in something that doesn't want to come. The frequency dropped. The three by the window settled, not knowing they'd moved.

Four seconds.

Mrs. Okafor was at the far side, refilling a tray. Someone laughed quietly at something said about <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> — not the laugh from the photograph, a different one. The nineteen hertz ran under all of it, low and steady, four beats of it keeping time before it eased back down and stayed.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> found the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> on the curb outside, both hands pressed over their ears. Not in distress, exactly — managing it. Elbows on their knees, spine gone rigid against the storefront, the careful posture of someone who'd done this before and knew the drill.

The hum was audible now without any help from his neuretics. Nineteen hertz, leaking out in waves that made the streetlight stutter, a frequency he could feel in his own teeth.

He sat down beside them. Not close. Close enough. He still had the plate. He hadn't come out here to fix anything — just to stay until the worst of it passed, and to make sure they didn't ride it out alone.

The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> didn't look at him. They kept their hands over their ears and stared at the wet concrete, where the rain came down clean and the runoff ran into the gutter at a steady rate.

"It's not one grief," the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> said. Their voice was controlled but close to the surface. "Forty griefs running at once. None of them the same frequency. Forty different ways of being broken about the same person, and I could feel all of it. All at once. Like standing in a room where every wall is playing a different song and you have to listen to all of them and not lose your mind."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set the plate on the curb beside him. The jollof rice had gone cold, the chicken still on it, untouched.

The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity>'s hands were shaking. Not tremor — actual shaking, the kind that comes when someone is holding a thing that wants to move through them and they're using every nerve to keep it in. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> ran down their face. They didn't wipe it.

"I don't know how you do this," the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> said. "Sit in a room full of people and just — be there. Let them feel whatever they're feeling and not try to fix it."

"You're doing it now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He recognized the breathing. Shallow, held, made small by force of will. He had done the same thing in the facility, back when the hardware was new and every thought that wasn't his own felt like drowning. You held your breath. You held your hands still. You made yourself small enough that maybe it would pass. He knew what it was to have a mind that was not entirely yours, and he knew the only relief was someone present who did not require you to explain it.

So he sat with the rain and the cold plate and the forty griefs, and he did not offer the gentle lies. Not *it gets easier*, not *you'll be fine*, none of the things people said when they didn't understand. He did not try to make any of it smaller.

A car passed, tires hissing on the wet asphalt. A woman with an umbrella gave them a wide berth and didn't look twice. The city moved around them, doing what it did when it wasn't paying attention.

He sat until it leveled. The nineteen hertz dipped lower — not gone, never gone tonight, but different now. Less like something trying to escape and more like something that had found a place to sit. The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity>'s shoulders came down a centimeter. And slowly their hands came down from their ears.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> found him at the end of the counter when the second round came around. She set a folded envelope beside his bowl without a word — heavy cream paper, the kind with a watermark pressed into it, the kind that cost money to feel that way. The letterhead read *<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s Antiquity & Stationary*, and under it a Dearborn address. The private entrance, not the counter-face number from the first time he'd stood at the shop.

Two words inside, no signature, in a hand that was not <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s — small, formal script, the writing of someone who had learned penmanship when it still mattered, back before the neural lace made the letters optional. Precise. Deliberate.

*Meet me.*

He read the two words and let them sit. Whoever sent this had put pen to paper and handed it to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> in person. That meant they had been here — at this counter, on a Thursday, at the wake. That kind of thing did not travel on relay channels; you could not intercept ink, could not subpoena a fold in cream paper, could not run a warrant on a thing that existed in only one copy in the world. That was the point of it. Someone knew where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went when he had nowhere else to be. Someone had moved through a room full of people trained to notice, found his coat among the others, and left the note so cleanly that no one had caught the edge of it. Someone had waited for the right room to hand him the paper, and had it ready before he walked in.

He folded the envelope once and put it in his coat. It felt heavier than paper should weigh. He finished his broth. The wok came back up like a bell, and the counter filled again with the sound of something ongoing, and he sat in it a while before he stood and said goodbye to the ones whose names he knew.

He did not know all of them.

title: The Address
text:
He had the address from <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s card. She kept a registration for the community that gathered that night, organized the way she organized everything, by district and block, and he'd read it on the way in out of habit. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s entry sat at the bottom. *<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>/Mimi T.* Registered the same careful way she did everything.

Six blocks from the carousel park. He hadn't put it together until he was standing at her door in the rain.

His neuretics were still running their baseline from the wake, and a line surfaced at the edge of his sight: AMBIENT INTERFERENCE — 18.9 HZ — TYPE UNCLASSIFIED. Point-two off the carousel. Same classification, same range. Two places six blocks apart on the same stretch of Halsted, both holding a note that nothing on either block had a reason to hold.

The cold came up off the wet stone into his hands. He stood at the door a moment. Then he went in.

title: The Vestibule
text:
The vestibule was quiet, the kind of quiet a place keeps only with effort. Old-spec ferrocement. The floor composite worn cold and smooth, stood on for decades by people nobody had bothered to replace it for.

The directory listed thirty-four names. On the third floor, one gap — a slot where the card had been pulled clean, nothing set back in its place.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand went to it before he decided anything. Two fingers, flat against the empty groove, the way you'd check a pulse that wasn't there. Somebody had come here and taken her name down. Not the building, not maintenance, not time. A person, with a tool, doing a small job carefully.

He knew this motion. He'd done it himself, once, on a slot that wasn't his to touch — cleaning a name off a directory so nobody would go looking for the room behind it. It worked. Nobody had gone looking for him in years.

The thought didn't come as a sentence. It came as heat behind his sternum and his jaw setting before he'd finished reading the empty slot, the specific stillness of a man recognizing his own handwriting in someone else's crime.

He took the stairs two at a time, boots loud on ferrocement that had absorbed forty years of footsteps and given none of them back.

The third-floor hallway smelled like machine oil and old rain, water finding its way in through a seam somewhere above the ceiling tile and staining a long brown tongue down the wall. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> ran down the doorframe ahead of him in two clean lines, one on each side of the jamb, like the building was crying in parallel. Null's door was unmarked — no number, which matched a woman who kept her own registration in cardstock code nobody else could read.

The lock was intact. Meridian 7-series, five-pin, no smart circuit — the kind of tumbler that had been standard here when the building still believed in privacy. That told him something. Whoever pulled the directory card hadn't needed to come inside — or hadn't wanted to, or hadn't finished. He crouched at the seam between door and frame, ran a thumb along the strip weatherproofing, checking for the fine grit of a forced re-seat. Clean. Untouched since she'd last closed it herself.

He knocked anyway. Once, correct, the way you knock on a door you already know is empty — not for her, for whoever might be listening on the other side of the wall, so they'd hear a caller behaving like a caller and nothing more.

No sound answered. No hum, no settle of floorboard, no breath of climate system cycling air through a room that still had someone paying its utility bill.

He put his palm flat against the door and held it there, and the cold of the composite came up through his hand the same way the cold from the wet stone outside <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s wake had come up into his fingers — the two temperatures matching, six blocks and one Thursday apart.

Whoever had scrubbed her name from the directory had left the room itself alone. That was a choice, not an oversight. A person who does the erasure in stages. A person who takes the public record down first and comes back later — or doesn't come back at all, because the public record was the only thing that mattered.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> straightened, and the small percentage of him that still ran cold math under everything else logged it without asking permission: *first the name, then the room, then the person.* He'd seen that order before. He'd used that order before.

He didn't have a key. He had a multitool clipped inside his jacket that could get him through this lock in under nine seconds — <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity> swollen a little with the wet, call it thirty if the rain had gotten into it — and he stood there in the hallway with his hand still on the wood, not reaching for it yet, weighing whether going in made this his to carry, the way carrying <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s body out of the dock had been his to carry, whether some things you didn't ask permission for either.

The building held its quiet around him, patient, unbothered, the kind of silence that had swallowed harder questions than his before.

title: The Room
text:
Mrs. Okafor had been there already. The candle in the window, the plate of food on the counter, still warm enough underneath to say she'd come within the last hour. She didn't cook for the dead. She cooked for the people the dead left behind.

The room was sparse in a way that said something about how <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> had lived — not poor, just without accumulation. No posters, no photographs, no evidence of anyone having lived here except in two facts the room was making at him from across the small floor.

The first was the work surface under the window. Tools laid out the way people who ran the Read laid out their materials: three soldering irons, tips cleaned and aligned, a set of calibration probes in a velvet roll, a magnifying lens on its articulated arm, a roll of solder with the end folded back on itself so the next person wouldn't have to hunt for where it started. Easy to reach, nothing for show, kept for use and for the record of use. The window faced east. When the first light came it would come through that glass at the right angle, and she would have known that when she took the room. She had positioned the table for a light that wasn't there yet. She had folded that solder back for hands that meant to return to it.

The second was the plate. Cream ceramic, the kind that held heat. Rice, chicken, a small heap of greens, a fork beside it tines down. A thin film of condensation on the rim where the steam had risen and then stopped rising. Someone had left this thinking somebody would come back to eat it.

Neither had accounted for what actually happened.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the center of it and touched nothing. He was aware of his hand at his side the way you're aware of a tool you're not using yet but might need. He could put the plate in the kitchenette. He could cover it. He could move one iron out of its row and make the room look like nobody had left anything out for someone who was never coming back.

He didn't do any of those things. It was still her room. It had the feel of a place that hadn't yet been told what it was now — the last moment before it became empty.

title: The Photograph
text:
The photograph was on the shelf above the work surface, in a cheap composite frame. He had come in to find the drive she'd hidden, and that was all he meant to do — pull the panel, take what she'd left him, and be gone before the light changed. Three people on a rooftop in summer, the elevated behind them, the light the specific kind you get in July or <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1706-719b-a8b8-26e0cdd6fb5e">August</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> was on the right, hair loose, holding a bottle, not looking at the camera. The other two were younger, or older than her; the photo didn't make it clear. All three were laughing at something outside the frame.

He set his fingers under the lip of the panel and pulled. It didn't give. He worked a nail into the seam and levered, and the composite flexed but held — screwed from the inside, not clipped, someone's careful precaution against exactly this. He pulled harder and the panel cracked along the grain, and the sound of it, sharp in the quiet, brought him up short. Down in the street a car door shut. Then another. He went still, and through the gap in the panel he could see the drive was not there at all — only a folded square of paper where the drive should have been, and voices now on the stair, two of them, coming up.

He had known her handle for three years. He had known her work. He had not known she had people she stood on rooftops with in summer. He looked at the photo a moment and let both names go. She was who she was. The handle was the name she'd offered him. It was the whole of it, and he had never asked for more.

title: The Read Slips
text:
The voices on the stair had passed the door without slowing — building maintenance, not for him — and by the time his pulse settled <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had gone back to the room. They sat in two stacks on the work surface, under a clear weight — half-size cardstock, the kind from the practitioners' supply shops in the old zone markets. Printed in the tight hand she used for everything: date codes at the top, classification marks she'd have worked out herself. The notation was private, the personal shorthand of someone who ran the Read for hire and kept careful records. Not for anyone else. For herself.

He didn't read them. Not because he couldn't work out the grammar — he'd known enough practitioners to have the general key — but because they were hers. Null being gone didn't change that.

He put his hand on the stack. Not picking it up. Just the weight of it under his palm — paper and cardstock, not much, but she'd ordered it, marked which slip came first, and that ordering was itself a thing that had been waiting. Her handwriting showed in the margin of the top slip: a date from three weeks before she died, and two words in her code. He didn't need to translate them. He knew what they meant.

She had known.

He came here to find the one thing she'd have left for him and no one else — proof of what she saw coming, in her own hand, and to carry it out before the others thought to search the room.

There was a folded note flat under the weight, his handle on the outside in her tight hand — not the careful block letters she used for job slips, but the faster shape you write when you're not performing for anyone. He opened it once.

*Before Broken Glass. Meant to tell you. The name I use — you do the same thing, smaller. Third try. It held.*

*Broken Glass.* Old street term for a Read gone feral, the architecture inside a psion's head fractured from holding too many minds at once. He didn't need the translation for that either. He put it in his coat.

title: The Psyk Outside
text:
A <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> sat in the stairwell on his way down — young, work clothes, a read-kit bag between their boots, two steps below the second-floor landing. Running the slow, controlled breath that pulls a sensitive's range back down under the ambient.

"It's strong here," they said. Not to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. To the fact of it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped on the landing. He'd come down for one thing: to get out of the building, out to the street, and put the whole floor behind him before whatever was up there settled any deeper into his chest. "Residual?"

"Running." The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> looked at the kit, then at the floor. "It knows the geometry. Been at it a while. Before tonight." Their fingers moved in a small calibration gesture, the kind practitioners make without noticing. "It's not malicious. It's just present — the way a signal's present when it's looking for something."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the stairwell door. Something in his neck had gone tight and would not let go. He said nothing else. He went out.

title: The Rain
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't go back inside.

He put one hand on <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> through the coat. Not drawing it. Just finding it — the weight, the shape, the matte-black edge, the tsuka wrap cord under his palm, cold through the coat. A confirmation that it was still there, still his, still real in the way objects are real when everything else has stopped making sense. He held his hand there a moment. Then he took it away.

The hum was gone.

Not faded. Not distant. Gone the way a sound goes when the source stops, complete and absolute. He hadn't caught the moment it stopped. All evening it had been in the room — the nineteen hertz, the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity>'s grief, the city's low baseline under both, braided into something with no clean name. The pressure in his teeth, the vibration in the base of his skull, the thing he'd learned to ignore the way you ignore your own heartbeat. Now it was gone between one breath and the next. The rain was just rain. Halsted was just Halsted.

And the rain was the cold kind, the redirected kind, carrying the chemical signature of the atmospheric processors' correction — sky money spent somewhere cleaner and the runoff sent down the south face of the elevated to fall on this. It ran down his face. He let it.

He wanted the relay under his hands and a job in the queue by morning — something with clean edges, something he could close. He walked north. The cold came off the synthesis corridor with nothing under it now but the city being the city: the electrical hum of the streetlights, a mag-truck thrumming three blocks over, the ordinary work of eight million people doing what they did when nobody was watching. The block would still be here in the morning. The people grieving inside would go home. The rain would keep coming down, the way it always had.

The relay was at home. There'd be a job on it. He walked.

title: The Second Entry
text:
The hum had stopped before he left the vestibule. By the time he cleared the elevated track and crossed onto Fullerton, his neuretics had dropped back to baseline. The cold did its ordinary work.

He was four blocks north when the notation appeared.

AMBIENT INTERFERENCE — 18.9 HZ — TYPE UNCLASSIFIED

Same class as the carousel.

He read it without breaking stride, the way he'd read the carousel one. The frequency sat below hearing. It didn't announce itself. His body just went alert — a low animal wariness with nothing to point at. He marked the cross-streets and kept walking. The rain was clean. The drains were working.

He tried to file it and move on, and couldn't. He queried the tag against his own logs — TYPE UNCLASSIFIED came back, which meant his neuretics had no referent, no prior, nothing to file it under. He pushed for a source vector. The system offered him a bearing, then revised it, then offered a third; the signal read as everywhere and nowhere, and each correction pulled his attention back to a street that held nothing worth watching. He ran a passive scan for a physical emitter — transformer, rail coupler, a bad ballast in a sign. Clean. The wariness had no object and would not resolve into one, and the harder he worked it the more it thinned into noise he could neither dismiss nor name. He gave up the query before it gave up on him.

The notation held for six blocks, then faded. That made three now: the carousel, the vestibule, and here — three weeks and change apart, different neighborhoods, the same tag. He let both sit where they were.

He got home. The relay had a new posting. Medical transport, short-haul, a loading dock in the south Loop — the kind of cover that moved things that weren't quite medical. The client field resolved to the same shell it always did. The rate was inside his range. He took it, confirmed the 0600 contact window, and closed the posting.

He went to bed. He did not think about the frequency.
